title: Blessed Virgin Mary of the Rosary
short_summary: Our Lady of the Rosary is a title of the Blessed Virgin Mary associated with the Rosary, a meditative prayer centered on the life, death, and Resurrection of Jesus Christ. The October 7 feast grew from the Christian victory at Lepanto in 1571 and has a special place in Dominican tradition.
key_facts: The Dominican Calendarium keeps the Blessed Virgin Mary of the Rosary as a feast on October 7.
The Rosary developed gradually during the second millennium, and Dominican preachers helped shape and spread its familiar form.
A commonly used Rosary consists of five decades, each built around an Our Father, ten Hail Marys, a Glory Be, and meditation on a mystery from the lives of Jesus and Mary.
Pope Pius V established the feast of Our Lady of Victory after the Battle of Lepanto on October 7, 1571; Gregory XIII later gave it the title Our Lady of the Rosary.
Saint John Paul II proposed the Luminous Mysteries in 2002, joining the traditional Joyful, Sorrowful, and Glorious Mysteries.

sections.heading: Origins and development
sections.body: The Rosary took shape over centuries from the Christian practice of repeating familiar prayers while meditating on the mysteries of salvation. Medieval forms were sometimes called a Marian Psalter because sets of Hail Marys offered ordinary Christians a pattern of prayer comparable to the 150 Psalms. By the late Middle Ages, Dominican preachers such as Blessed Alan de la Roche were organizing Rosary confraternities and promoting the devotion across Europe.

sections.heading: Saint Dominic and the Dominican Order
sections.body: Catholic tradition closely associates the Rosary with Saint Dominic and the Order of Preachers. The modern prayer developed after Dominic's lifetime, but Dominicans played a central role in its formation and spread. The Rosary became a characteristic part of Dominican life, worn on the habit and used to join contemplation of Christ with the Order's mission of preaching.

sections.heading: Lepanto and the feast
sections.body: In 1571 Pope Pius V asked Christians to pray the Rosary while the Holy League confronted the Ottoman fleet at Lepanto. The fleet's victory on October 7 was attributed to Mary's intercession. Pius established a feast of Our Lady of Victory in thanksgiving, and Gregory XIII later renamed it Our Lady of the Rosary. Clement XI extended the observance to the universal Church in the early eighteenth century, and Saint Pius X fixed its date as October 7 in 1913.

sections.heading: Prayers and mysteries
sections.body: Each decade of the Rosary combines spoken prayer with meditation on a mystery from the Gospel. The Joyful Mysteries concern Christ's infancy, the Luminous Mysteries his public ministry, the Sorrowful Mysteries his Passion, and the Glorious Mysteries his Resurrection and the life of the Church. Saint John Paul II proposed the Luminous Mysteries in 2002 to give greater attention to the years between Christ's Baptism and Passion.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: A Christ-centered Marian prayer
catholic_connection_sections.body: The Hail Mary gives the Rosary its Marian form, but Jesus is the center of every mystery. Catholics pray with Mary while contemplating her Son, from the Annunciation and Nativity through the Cross, Resurrection, Ascension, and the sending of the Holy Spirit.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Scripture and contemplation
catholic_connection_sections.body: The mysteries provide a framework for returning repeatedly to the events of the Gospel. The repetition of the prayers supplies a steady rhythm while the mind attends to Christ's words and deeds.

catholic_connection_sections.heading: Dominican prayer and preaching
catholic_connection_sections.body: Dominican spirituality joins contemplation to preaching. The Rosary gathers the principal mysteries of Christ into a form of prayer that can also teach, preserve, and proclaim the Gospel.

historical_cautions: The traditional account of Mary personally giving the Rosary to Saint Dominic appears in sources written well after his death. Describe it as Dominican or Catholic tradition rather than as a securely dated historical event.
